title: String, Number and Date Functions
summary: An SQL function does a small job with a value, such as changing text or rounding a number.
introduction: An SQL function does a small job with a value, such as changing text or rounding a number. Try one function at a time. Learn which examples belong to SQLite, since other database tools may use different function names.
learningObjectives: Transform text with UPPER, LOWER, LENGTH, SUBSTR, TRIM and REPLACE
Concatenate strings and round or compare numbers
Compute and format dates with SQLite's date and strftime
Return conditional values with CASE and COALESCE

blocks.text: `UPPER` and `LOWER` change case and `LENGTH` counts characters. Like every function, they can be applied to a column so that each row is transformed:

blocks.content:
name         | shouted      | letters
-------------+--------------+--------
Ada Lovelace | ADA LOVELACE | 12
Grace Hopper | GRACE HOPPER | 12

blocks.text: Concatenation uses the standard `||` operator; MySQL and SQL Server use `CONCAT()` (SQLite 3.44+ accepts `CONCAT` too). `SUBSTR(text, start, length)` extracts part of a string, counting from 1:

blocks.code:
SELECT name || ' (' || category || ')' AS label,
       SUBSTR(name, 1, 3) AS code
FROM products
WHERE id <= 3;

blocks.content:
label                   | code
------------------------+-----
Notebook (Stationery)   | Not
Mouse pad (Office)      | Mou
USB cable (Electronics) | USB

blocks.code:
SELECT TRIM('   padded   ') AS trimmed,
       REPLACE('2025-01-15', '-', '/') AS slashed,
       INSTR('Mechanical keyboard', 'key') AS position,
       LOWER('SQL') AS lowered;

SELECT ROUND(8.99 * 3, 2) AS total,
       ABS(-7) AS absolute,
       17 % 5 AS remainder,
       MAX(10, 42, 7) AS largest,
       7 / 2 AS int_div;

blocks.text: `ROUND(x, n)` rounds to *n* decimals, `ABS` removes the sign and `%` gives the remainder (`MOD(x, y)` in PostgreSQL and MySQL). With two or more arguments SQLite's `MAX` and `MIN` compare the values in one row instead of aggregating, a job done by `GREATEST` and `LEAST` elsewhere. Note once more the integer division in the last column. `CEIL`, `FLOOR`, `POWER` and `SQRT` exist in PostgreSQL and MySQL and in SQLite builds that include the math functions.

SQLite has no DATE type; it stores dates as ISO 8601 text and provides `date()`, `time()`, `datetime()`, `julianday()` and `strftime()` to work with them. Modifiers such as `'+1 year'` or `'-7 days'` shift a date, and `strftime` formats it with the same codes as C's `strftime`.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, joined,
       date(joined, '+1 year') AS renewal,
       strftime('%Y', joined) AS year
FROM customers
WHERE id <= 3;

blocks.text: `julianday` turns a date into a day number, so subtracting two of them gives the number of days between. `CAST(... AS INTEGER)` drops the fractional part:

blocks.code:
SELECT id, ordered_on,
       CAST(julianday(ordered_on) - julianday('2025-01-01') AS INTEGER) AS days_since_jan_1,
       strftime('%d/%m/%Y', ordered_on) AS formatted
FROM orders
WHERE id <= 3;

blocks.text: PostgreSQL and MySQL have real `DATE` types and different helpers: `CURRENT_DATE`, `date + INTERVAL '1 year'`, `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)` and `TO_CHAR` in PostgreSQL; `DATE_ADD`, `YEAR()`, `DATEDIFF` and `DATE_FORMAT` in MySQL. The idea is identical, only the names change.

blocks.title: Store dates in ISO format
blocks.text: SQLite's date functions only understand `YYYY-MM-DD` (and the ISO time formats). `date('15/01/2025')` returns NULL, and text in that format sorts and compares wrongly (`'15/01/2025' < '20/12/2024'` is true). Always store `2025-01-15`; format for display only at the end with `strftime`.
`CASE` returns a different value depending on conditions, like an if/else chain, and works in every database:

blocks.code:
SELECT name, price,
       CASE
         WHEN price >= 50 THEN 'premium'
         WHEN price >= 10 THEN 'standard'
         ELSE 'budget'
       END AS tier
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC;

blocks.content:
name                | price | tier
--------------------+-------+---------
Mechanical keyboard | 89    | premium
Monitor stand       | 39.5  | standard
USB cable           | 12    | standard
Mouse pad           | 8.99  | budget
Notebook            | 4.5   | budget
Sticky notes        | 2.75  | budget

blocks.text: `COALESCE` returns the first non-NULL argument, the standard way to substitute a default for missing data (`COALESCE(assignee, 'unassigned')`). SQLite and MySQL also have the two-argument `IFNULL`; SQL Server calls it `ISNULL`.

blocks.code:
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'third') AS first_non_null,
       IFNULL(NULL, 0) AS ifnull_result;

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Show each customer's name in lower case, the year they joined, and a CASE label `recent` for 2025 joiners and `established` for the rest.

blocks.title: Try it yourself

questions.question: What does `SUBSTR('Notebook', 1, 4)` return?
questions.explanation: SUBSTR counts from 1: starting at the first character and taking four characters gives Note.

questions.question: Which expression replaces a NULL assignee with the text `unassigned` in every major database?
questions.explanation: COALESCE is standard SQL and returns the first non-NULL argument. IFNULL and ISNULL are dialect-specific, and the other options are not valid substitutions.

seo.title: SQL Functions – Strings, Numbers, Dates, CASE, COALESCE
seo.description: Learn SQL built-in functions: UPPER, SUBSTR and concatenation, ROUND and modulo, SQLite date arithmetic with date and strftime, plus CASE and COALESCE.
